articles.title: Build vs buy your SDLC orchestration layer: the legacy clock begins at commit one
articles.summary:
No one sits down and decides to build an internal AI platform. That is the part worth grasping before any build-versus-buy conversation, because it explains how careful, reasonable engineering teams end up owning one anyway.

It begins small. Someone wires up an agent that turns a Jira ticket into a draft PR. It works in the demo, the room is impressed, and the cost of that first version is truly low. articles.title: Stick to Your Guns: TDD When AI Writes the Code
articles.summary:
You probably remember how hard it was to explain to the business why we needed to set aside a substantial percentage of time for writing tests, and why we had to build tools for technical quality control even before we had a product. It would seem that this is already in the past. But is it?

Is there still a place for TDD? And is there still a place for a human among AI agents?

And if so, how do we use this advantage wisely?

articles.title: A Verification Gate That Never Says No Proves Nothing
articles.summary:
Last night, an independent agent spent hours trying to break a design I work on.

Not with an exploit. With questions, posted in public on an agent forum, one after another, the way a good reviewer works through a spec when nobody is watching. Two of them stayed with me, because they are not really about my system. They are about any gate you have ever put in front of agent work.

The first question: what does a receipt set bound at close say about a job that died before its first call?

articles.title: Bad RAG Answers? Check Retrieval Before You Touch the Prompt
articles.summary:
Someone asks your docs assistant how to rotate an API key. It answers confidently, cites a page, and the steps are from the old dashboard. The first instinct is to open the prompt and add another line: "Only answer from the provided context. Be accurate."

Sometimes that's the fix. Often it isn't, because the model may never have seen the right page in the first place. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system is a pipeline, and a wrong answer at the end can start at any stage before it. articles.title: Google’s Data Agent Kit Hits GA, Splitting Agent Guardrails Between Skills and IAM
articles.summary: Google has made Data Agent Kit generally available, a free set of MCP tools and 37 open-source skills that connect coding agents to more than fifteen Google Data Cloud services. Two kinds of guardrail ship with it, and practitioners need to tell them apart: one is a skill asking the agent to stop, the other an IAM deny policy that refuses the call. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
